content: Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is a method of neonatal care that involves skin-to-skin contact between a mother and her newborn, frequent and exclusive or nearly exclusive breastfeeding, and early discharge from the hospital. It has been proposed as an alternative to conventional neonatal care for low birthweight (LBW) infants. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether KMC is supported by evidence as an alternative to conventional neonatal care, either before or after the initial stabilization period, and to assess its benefits and potential adverse effects. The review included a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, and POPLINE, as well as the WHO Trial Registration Data Set, up to June 30, 2016. Additional sources, such as the Kangaroo Foundation website, conference proceedings, and Google Scholar, were also searched. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials comparing KMC with conventional neonatal care or early-onset KMC with late-onset KMC in LBW infants. A total of 21 studies involving 3,042 infants met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 19 studies evaluated KMC after stabilization, one study evaluated KMC before stabilization, and one study compared early-onset KMC with late-onset KMC in relatively stable LBW infants. Sixteen studies assessed intermittent KMC, while five studies assessed continuous KMC. When comparing KMC to conventional neonatal care, the following findings were observed: 1. Mortality Reduction: At discharge or at 40 to 41 weeks' postmenstrual age, KMC significantly reduced the risk of mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.39 to 0.92; eight trials, 1,736 infants). At the latest follow-up, KMC was also associated with a reduced risk of mortality (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.95; 12 trials, 2,293 infants). 2. Infection and Sepsis: KMC significantly reduced the risk of nosocomial infection or sepsis (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.54; five trials, 1,239 infants) and severe infection or sepsis at the latest follow-up (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.69; eight trials, 1,463 infants). 3. Hypothermia: KMC was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of hypothermia (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.49; nine trials, 989 infants). 4. Growth Parameters: KMC improved weight gain (mean difference [MD] 4.1 g/day, 95% CI 2.3 to 5.9; 11 trials, 1,198 infants), length gain (MD 0.21 cm/week, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.38; three trials, 377 infants), and head circumference gain (MD 0.14 cm/week, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.22; four trials, 495 infants). 5. Breastfeeding: KMC increased the likelihood of exclusive breastfeeding at discharge or at 40 to 41 weeks' postmenstrual age (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.25; six studies, 1,453 mothers) and at one to three months' follow-up (RR 1.20, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.43; five studies, 600 mothers). It also increased the likelihood of any breastfeeding (exclusive or partial) at discharge or at 40 to 41 weeks' postmenstrual age (RR 1.20, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.34; 10 studies, 1,696 mothers) and at one to three months' follow-up (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.31; nine studies, 1,394 mothers). 6. Mother-Infant Attachment: KMC was associated with improvements in some measures of mother-infant attachment and the home environment. No significant differences were observed between KMC and conventional care in psychomotor development at 12 months' corrected age, as measured by Griffith quotients (low-quality evidence). Sensitivity analyses indicated that the inclusion of studies with a high risk of bias did not alter the overall findings or the magnitude of the treatment effects. When comparing early-onset KMC (initiated within 24 hours of birth) with late-onset KMC (initiated after 24 hours of birth) in relatively stable LBW infants, one trial involving 73 infants found no significant differences in mortality, morbidity, severe infection, hypothermia, breastfeeding, or nutritional indicators. However, early-onset KMC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in the length of hospital stay (MD 0.9 days, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.2). In conclusion, the evidence supports the use of KMC as an alternative to conventional neonatal care for LBW infants, particularly in resource-limited settings. However, further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of early-onset continuous KMC in unstabilized or relatively stabilized LBW infants, as well as its long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes and cost implications.
